title: API Inspector Training on the West Coast: CA, WA, OR and AK
description: Self-paced online API 510, 570, 580 and 653 exam prep for West Coast inspectors, with instructor Q&A. Refineries, terminals and California and Washington rules.
h1: API Inspector Training on the West Coast: Exam Prep for California, Washington, Oregon and Alaska Inspectors
html:
API inspector training for West Coast refineries and terminals

The West Coast has fewer refineries than the Gulf, but it asks more of the inspectors who work in them. California and Washington both run refinery-specific process safety rules that go beyond the federal standard, Alaska adds cold service and long distances, and Oregon, with no refinery at all, depends on terminals and pipelines that need tank inspectors. This page is for inspectors, NDT technicians, welders, operators and engineers in those states who are preparing for API 510, API 570, API 580 or API 653.

Atlantis's offices are in Houston and Hyderabad, and there is no Atlantis classroom in California, Washington, Oregon or Alaska. The exam-prep courses are self-paced and online, with instructor Q&A, so the material is the same wherever you log in. The American Petroleum Institute decides eligibility, administers the examinations, in person at Prometric test centres for API 510, 570 and 653 and at a centre or by remote proctoring for API 580, and issues each certification. Atlantis is not an API-approved training provider.

Where API inspectors work on the West Coast

EIA's refinery capacity survey for the start of 2026 lists 12 operating refineries in California with about 1.5 million barrels per calendar day of crude distillation capacity, five in Washington with about 648,000, five in Alaska with about 177,000 and one in Hawaii. Oregon has none: according to the Oregon Department of Energy, the state imports all of its refined liquid fuels, and more than 90% of the transportation fuel it uses is refined in Washington.

Hawaii's single refinery, operated by Par Hawaii at Kapolei, rounds out the Pacific picture. In Washington, the five refineries cluster in the north of Puget Sound and at Tacoma, so an inspector based in Seattle or Bellingham can reach all of them in a day's drive.

Fewer refineries, steady inspection work

California's refinery count has fallen. EIA reports that Phillips 66 stopped refining at its Los Angeles plant in October 2025, a cut of about 5% in West Coast refining capacity, and that Valero's Benicia refinery has also stopped refining and was removed from EIA's monthly estimates in March 2026. Phillips 66 stopped processing crude at Rodeo in early 2024 and now runs the site on renewable feedstocks, according to Argus.

That does not empty the job market for inspectors. The remaining refineries still run their vessels, piping and tanks under mechanical integrity programmes, and a converted plant still has pressure equipment and piping that someone has to inspect. EIA also points out that West Coast refinery cuts weigh more heavily on supply because pipeline links from the Gulf Coast are limited. Fuel that is not refined in the region arrives by ship, and every marine terminal that receives it has tanks, dock lines and manifolds for API 653 and API 570 inspectors to look after.

California's refinery rules and what they ask of inspectors

California's refineries work under Title 8, section 5189.1, Cal/OSHA's process safety management standard for petroleum refineries, in force since October 2017. It applies to sites in NAICS code 324110 and replaces the general PSM section for them. Several parts land directly on the inspection department.

  • Damage mechanism review (subsection k). Each process where a damage mechanism exists needs a DMR, carried out by a team that includes expertise in equipment and pipe inspection, damage and failure mechanisms and process operations. The review covers process flow, likely damage mechanisms, material suitability, prevention and mitigation, and operating parameters, and it must be revalidated at least every five years. A DMR is also required before approving a major change that may introduce a new damage mechanism.
  • Mechanical integrity (subsection j). Inspections and tests must follow procedures that meet or exceed recognized and generally accepted good engineering practice, at a frequency consistent with those practices or a more protective internal standard. The record of each inspection has to show the date, the inspector, what was done, the results and the equipment identifier.
  • Hierarchy of hazard controls and safeguard protection analyses. These are engineering analyses rather than inspection tasks, but their recommendations often turn into inspection and monitoring actions that an inspector then has to carry out and document.

Section 5189.1 does not name API codes; it mentions API only as an example of an organisation whose publications count as good engineering practice. In practice the inspection codes are how California refiners show that their inspection and testing meet that test. Cal/OSHA's Process Safety Management unit enforces the rule.

Two other California rules shape the calendar and the paperwork. The California Energy Commission requires refiners to file a planned maintenance report at least 120 days before a planned turnaround, and the turnaround schedule given to the Commission has to match the one notified to Cal/OSHA. Outside refinery PSM, Cal/OSHA's Pressure Vessel Unit issues permits to operate for air tanks above 1.5 cubic feet, LP-gas tanks above 125 gallons and power boilers above 15 psig, while Title 8 section 467(b) leaves the owner responsible for whatever inspection and maintenance its other vessels need to operate safely.

Washington's refinery PSM rule and pressure vessel certificates

Washington followed California's lead. The Department of Labor and Industries added a refinery-specific Part B to chapter 296-67 WAC, adopted in December 2023 and effective from December 2024. Like the California rule it requires damage mechanism reviews for processes where damage mechanisms exist, with at least half of the initial reviews due within three years of the effective date and the rest within five, and it requires hierarchy of hazard controls analyses revalidated at least every five years, a human factors programme and a process safety culture assessment.

Washington also regulates unfired pressure vessels through its boiler and pressure vessel program. Under WAC 296-104-125, a covered boiler or unfired pressure vessel has to be inspected by an inspector and hold the necessary permits before L&I issues a certificate of inspection, and the process is not complete until the certificate is posted. Refinery inspectors in Anacortes, Ferndale and Tacoma therefore work with two layers: the owner's API-based programme and the state's certificate regime. Find out which equipment at your site falls under each before you assume one inspection satisfies both.

Damage mechanisms and design details West Coast inspectors study

West Coast service conditions differ from the Gulf's, and the differences show up in which parts of the Body of Knowledge feel familiar.

  • Seismic design of tanks. Tanks in California, Washington and Alaska are commonly designed for earthquake loads, and API 650's seismic annex governs details such as anchorage. API 653 inspectors here deal with anchor bolts, anchor chairs and seismic freeboard on the tanks themselves.
  • Wet marine climate. Long wet winters around Puget Sound and the bays keep insulation damp, so corrosion under insulation and external chloride cracking of austenitic stainless steel are everyday concerns. The API RP 583 explainer summarises the CUI guidance.
  • Hydroprocessing and high-temperature service. Hydroprocessing units, common in refineries that make low-sulfur fuels, bring high temperature hydrogen attack (API RP 941) and sulfidation into the inspection plan. Both are catalogued in API RP 571, the damage mechanism reference that sits behind every DMR.
  • Cold service in Alaska. Low ambient temperatures make brittle fracture a practical concern. API 653 has a section on brittle fracture considerations for tanks, and API 510 candidates study minimum design metal temperature and impact test exemption rules from ASME Section VIII.
  • Changing feedstocks. Plants that switch between crude grades or move to renewable feeds can introduce damage mechanisms the original design never saw, which is exactly the situation the California rule's DMR-before-major-change requirement addresses.

Owners who need a damage mechanism review or risk-based inspection study rather than training can see the damage mechanism review and RBI in Los Angeles and Long Beach pages.

Which API certification fits West Coast work

  • Refinery unit inspectors in the Los Angeles basin, the Bay Area and Puget Sound need API 510 and API 570, and the documentation demands of section 5189.1 and Washington's Part B reward inspectors who can read the codes closely.
  • Inspectors moving into DMR and RBI teams add API 580 and often API 571. Because both state rules require damage mechanism reviews with inspection expertise on the team, an inspector who understands RBI concepts is useful well beyond turnaround season.
  • Terminal and tank farm inspectors at the ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach, around the bays, at the Portland Terminal Cluster and at Alaskan tank farms need API 653, often with API 570 for dock and manifold piping.
  • Inspectors on the North Slope and in the Central Valley see production and processing equipment where owners often apply API 510 and API 570 to vessels and piping, and API 653 to tankage.

Many West Coast inspectors come from NDT and welding. Atlantis's ASNT NDT training pages for Los Angeles, the San Francisco Bay Area, Seattle, Tacoma, Bakersfield, Oregon and Alaska describe the earlier steps, and the Los Angeles and Seattle AWS CWI exam-prep pages cover the welding inspector route.

Studying for an API exam from the West Coast

Self-paced study removes the time-zone problem. Candidates in Pacific, Alaska and Hawaii time study when it suits them and send questions to the instructor whenever they hit a problem; the answer comes back from the code text rather than at a fixed class hour. Three habits help West Coast candidates in particular.

  1. Use the turnaround calendar. California refiners report planned turnarounds to the Energy Commission months ahead, so most candidates there can see their busy months coming. Put the exam window between them.
  2. Read the state rule beside the code. Knowing what section 5189.1 or Washington's Part B asks of your site makes the exam's API 571 and API 580 material far easier to remember, because you can attach each mechanism to a review you have seen.
  3. Plan the trip to the test centre. Prometric lists test centres in and around the main West Coast metro areas. Candidates in remote Alaska, the Central Valley or eastern Washington may need to travel, so book early in the window and allow a night away if the appointment starts in the morning.

Eligibility is the same everywhere: education plus documented experience on the equipment, gained in the last 10 years in work for or under contract with an authorized inspection agency. The API 510, API 570 and API 653 certification pages set out the full scale, and API 580 is automatic for anyone holding a current 510, 570 or 653.

West Coast employers sponsoring API candidates

Refiners preparing more inspectors for DMR work, contractors staffing Bay Area and Puget Sound turnarounds and terminal operators building tank inspection coverage can enrol several candidates together, preparing for different API exams if needed. Fees are quoted on request. Each candidate applies to API individually and studies at their own pace with the instructor. Owners who need NDE and data review on their equipment can see the API 510 vessel inspection support in California, API 570 piping inspection support in Washington and API 653 tank inspection support in California pages.

faq.q: Is there an Atlantis classroom in Los Angeles or the Bay Area?
faq.a: No. There is no Atlantis classroom in Los Angeles, the Bay Area or anywhere else on the West Coast; Atlantis's offices are in Houston and Hyderabad. The API 510, 570, 580 and 653 exam-prep courses are self-paced online courses with instructor Q&A, so you can study around refinery shifts and turnarounds. You sit API 510, 570 or 653 at a Prometric test centre once API has accepted your application; API 580 can also be remotely proctored.

faq.q: Does California's refinery PSM rule require API certification?
faq.a: Section 5189.1 does not name specific API codes or certifications. It requires inspections and tests that meet or exceed recognized and generally accepted good engineering practice, and it mentions API as an example of an organisation whose publications count. California refiners typically meet that requirement through API 510, API 570 and API 653 programmes, so the owner decides which certifications its inspectors and contractors must hold. Ask the site before you take on a scope.

faq.q: Why does a damage mechanism review matter for API 580 candidates?
faq.a: California's section 5189.1 and Washington's refinery PSM rule both require damage mechanism reviews, with inspection expertise on the review team. The review identifies how each piece of equipment can deteriorate, which is the foundation of probability of failure in a risk-based inspection programme. API 580 candidates who have taken part in a DMR usually find the exam's concepts of damage mechanisms, inspection effectiveness and reassessment triggers much easier to follow.

faq.q: Are there API inspector jobs in Oregon if the state has no refineries?
faq.a: Yes, mainly in tank and terminal work. Oregon imports all of its refined fuels; more than 90% of its transportation fuel comes from Washington refineries, with the Olympic Pipeline as the backbone of supply, and the Portland Terminal Cluster is the state's primary storage for petroleum products. Terminal tanks need API 653 inspection, and the piping that connects them to docks and pipelines is API 570 work.

faq.q: Does Washington regulate unfired pressure vessels?
faq.a: Yes. Washington's Department of Labor and Industries runs a boiler and unfired pressure vessel program. Under WAC 296-104-125, a covered vessel must be inspected by an inspector and hold the necessary permits before a certificate of inspection is issued, and the certificate has to be posted. That sits alongside the owner's own API 510 inspection programme, so refinery inspectors in Washington should know which vessels fall under the state regime.

faq.q: Can I prepare for API 653 from Alaska?
faq.a: Yes. The course is online and self-paced, so location only matters on exam day. Instructor Q&A works around Alaska time because you send questions when you study rather than at a set hour. Alaskan tank work also brings cold-service topics, such as brittle fracture considerations in API 653, into everyday practice. Plan your Prometric appointment early, since candidates outside Anchorage may need to travel to a test centre.

faq.q: Can a West Coast employer sponsor several candidates?
faq.a: Yes. Refiners, contractors and terminal operators can enrol several candidates, including candidates preparing for different API exams, and fees are quoted on request. Each candidate applies to API individually with their own experience record and studies at their own pace. Tell us which exams, which windows and how many candidates when you enquire, and keep each candidate's exam window clear of their turnaround assignments.
